stories.title: SF, SNP, Welsh leaders sign deal pushing for independence
stories.summary: The leaders of Sinn Féin, the SNP, and Plaid Cymru have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end" in a joint agreement aimed at putting pressure on Downing Street to hold referendums on independence. The first ministers of the UK's three devolved nations - SNP leader John Swinney, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth and Sinn Féin leader in Northern Ireland Michelle O'Neill - signed the memorandum of understanding during a meeting in Cardiff this morning. Along with Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald, the leaders called on the British government to "prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change". The group, who met in their capacity as party leaders - rather than as officials in their respective governments, also stated their ambitions for partnership around the economy, energy and international co-operation. The agreement says: "The political landscape across these islands is changing. "For the first time ever, people across these islands have first ministers in Scotland, in Wales and in the North of Ireland who are all committed to independence from the United Kingdom.

stories.title: Trump visit is on par heading down the final fairway
stories.summary: A day of Dublin diplomacy for US President Donald Trump passed largely without drama, with the Government spared his usual political fire. However, he turned the spotlight back on a united Ireland and delivered an awkward moment that became the focus for Irish and UK politicians. At the start of yesterday, all eyes were on his meeting with President Catherine Connolly, and whether she would get under his skin by raising issues, including war and genocide, as well as her previous highly critical comments about his conduct in office. Saturday had started with what appeared to be a mostly pleasant courtesy call to President Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, with President Trump describing her as "terrific" during a later speech at the US Ambassador's residence. An Oval Office-style Q&A with the media took place not in Washington but at Farmleigh House, where the Taoiseach and President Trump held bilateral talks. Questions took on the big headline stories that have dominated Mr Trump’s second term, including Iran and Gaza, along with his highly anticipated meeting with President Connolly.

stories.title: Toibín targets dozen Aontú seats, rules out FG coalition
stories.summary: Aontú leader Peadar Toibín has told his party's think-in that it is targeting up to a dozen seats in the next Dáil election. Speaking at the event in Co Derry this morning, Mr Toibín referenced recent polling which put his party at 8% of the vote. He said that could translate into a decent number of seats at the next election. He told delegates that a dozen seats was not impossible "on a good day", and that Aontú had very strong chances in constituencies like Cavan/Monaghan, Meath East, Dublin West, Wexford and Limerick City. He said he believed the party's strong showing at the polls was happening because it was "listening to the people" and that others had lost touch with their base. He ruled out going into government with Fine Gael after the next election and while he said they would "find it very difficult to put Micheál Martin back into power", the likelihood was that he might have been replaced by his party by then.

stories.title: Oil up 3% after new strikes on Saudi, Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: Oil prices rose about 3% today, after new strikes on Saudi Arabian energy and civilian infrastructure and Iranian attacks on ships in the Gulf compounded supply concerns following the closure of a key Saudi oil pipeline. Brent crude futures climbed $2.93, or 2.8%, to $107.54 per barrel this morning, while WTI futures gained $2.88, or 2.9%, to $102.93 per barrel. "This follows a step-up in attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure, including targeting the crucial East-West pipeline," said ING commodity strategists, though they noted it was unclear how severe any potential damage was or how long the pipeline would be out of action. Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline was temporarily shut following a drone attack, according to Saudi officials. The shutdown of the pipeline, which helps Saudi Arabia avoid the Strait of Hormuz and re-route its exports, threatens up to 4% of global oil supply. With the pipeline out of service, the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea has enough inventory to cover just five to seven days of exports, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi Arabia's exports. Saudi Arabian state media yesterday released video footage of damage to homes and a mosque from what it said was a Houthi attack on the country's southern Jazan province. The Houthis said they had also struck a Saudi military base in a neighbouring province.

stories.title: UK should rejoin EU customs union, Osborne says
stories.summary: Former British chancellor George Osborne has said the UK's economy has "fallen off a cliff" since Brexit and that rejoining the EU customs union would be the fastest route to recovery. Mr Osborne, who resigned as chancellor after being part of David Cameron's cabinet at the time of the referendum, said it was important to rebuild links with the EU. "Brexit has been a mess," he said in an interview with The Independent. "It has had a huge impact on the British economy. It is clearly poorer than it would otherwise be," he said. Acknowledging that rejoining the EU would be difficult a decade on from the Brexit referendum, Mr Osborne said closer ties with Europe can boost the economy. "I would rejoin the customs union," he said. "It's a quite simple thing to do. That was never part of the Brexit debate. No one knew we were leaving it and it has had a devastating impact on trade.

stories.summary: Antrim clubs Loughgiel and St John's will await their fate after violent scenes marred their senior hurling clash at Fr Healy Park. The group encounter, a repeat of last year’s county final, passed off without any major incident over the course of 63 minutes, with reigning champions St John’s losing out 3-14 to 0-30. Both sides advanced to the knockout stages in a game that saw just three yellow cards handed out. At the full-time whistle however tempers flared between both panels. Initially players and mentors on both sides clashed in the middle of the pitch, before footage from the ground shows how things escalated further with the violence spilling over into the crowd. The clubs will now await any proposed penalties resulting from the action.

stories.title: RTÉ Culture series 100 Buildings inspires new architecture book
stories.summary: This Modern Love: Architectural Gems of 20th Century Ireland, by architectural historian Emma Gilleece, will be published by Gill Books on 23 October. The series has featured a range of building types, including schools, hospitals, government offices, factories, churches and transport buildings. Buildings examined include the original terminal at Dublin Airport, the Poolbeg Chimneys in Dublin, the former Kildare Fever Hospital in Naas, the Padmore and Barnes boot factory in Kilkenny and the original CIÉ bus station in Clonmel. More recent entries have included the Cork Distillers Bottling Plant on North Mall in Cork, the Department of Trade, Enterprise and Employment on Kildare Street in Dublin and a Modernist vocational school building in Dungarvan, Co Waterford. Gilleece’s articles have also examined the influence of social change and government policy on Irish architecture. An article on the former fever hospital in Naas looked at the State’s hospital-building programme of the 1930s, while the piece on the Padmore and Barnes factory explored the Irish Free State’s drive for industrial development and self-sufficiency. The original Dublin Airport terminal, completed in 1940, was examined in the context of the development of civil aviation in Ireland.

stories.title: Roscommon woman crowned Best Dressed at The Curragh
stories.summary: Laura Hanlon from Co Roscommon was crowned Best Dressed at The Curragh's final style competition of 2026. Judged by Mayo content creator Sarah Butler of Sarah Butler at Home and renowned stylist and broadcaster Marietta Doran, Grace & Glory invited participants to express their "own unapologetic sense of style" while taking on the "bold spirit of Grace O'Malley". In the end, the judges selected Hanlon's daring red look, which came with some impressively sustainable accessories. The designer wore a three-piece ensemble from Phoenix V in Cork, paired with shoes that she sourced from Vinted for just €4. Most impressively, she made her statement headpiece and bag especially for the day. The red scalloped bag was made from a box of Nature Valley bars that was destined for the recycling bin. As well as the coveted title of Best Dressed, Laura was awarded a stay at The Grace, Westport Estate - including two nights’ bed and breakfast in the Grace Kelly Suite, à la carte dining with champagne at Black Sheep, two signature spa treatments, and a half-day Chauffeur-driven tour of Clew Bay and Achill Island.

stories.title: Whiskey tariff removal for 'just Ireland', not EU - Trump
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has said yesterday evening's move to lift tariffs on Irish whiskey applies to Ireland only and not the EU. Whiskey made in the Republic of Ireland that is sold into the US was subject to a 10% tariff, putting it at a disadvantage with Scotch and Northern Irish whiskey which currently has no tariff. Mr Trump announced the move at the end of the Irish Open in Doonbeg in Co Clare yesterday. His announcement has been welcomed by the Government and by the representatives of the Irish whiskey industry. On the tarmac at Shannon Airport before leaving for the United States on Air Force One yesterday evening, Mr Trump was asked whether it would apply only to Ireland or across the EU. "It was very unfair because others had the relief and they didn't, so I thought I'd do it. Actually, Shane [Lowry] asked me about it, too. A lot of people asked me."

stories.title: Trump unity remarks reflect broad US sentiment - Adams
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump's remarks in support of Irish unity reflect the "broad north American sentiment", former Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams has said. Mr Adams welcomed Mr Trump's remarks but stated that Taoiseach Micheál Martin had "put himself outside this positive attitude" towards holding a border poll. The US president is currently on a two-day visit to Ireland. Yesterday, during a meeting with Mr Martin, Mr Trump claimed Irish reunification was inevitable, adding it "may as well happen now". "But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?" During a subsequent engagement at the US Ambassador's residence in Ireland, Mr Trump did not back away from his earlier answer, stating Irish unification would be "a very cool thing". Mr Adams, who was the Sinn Féin leader when the Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998, delivered a speech in Dublin today reflecting on the peace deal.

stories.title: Ulster Unionists select candidate for Doug Beattie's seat
stories.summary: The Ulster Unionist Party has selected Kyle Savage as its candidate for next year's Assembly elections in the constituency represented by former party leader Doug Beattie. Upper Bann MLA Mr Beattie resigned from the party in May, citing a "toxic atmosphere" under its current leadership, and now sits as an independent unionist. Party leader Jon Burrows said Mr Savage "will have the full backing of the party" when he runs in the constituency. Mr Savage is a twice deputy lord mayor of Armagh City, Banbridge and Craigavon. Mr Burrows said: "He was selected by our members in Upper Bann because they know him, trust him and want him to be their voice at Stormont. "This is a constituency that punches above its weight, and it deserves a representative who is part of a team working together to make Northern Ireland stronger and more successful.

stories.title: How your travel plans have changed because of wars and warzones
stories.summary: Analysis: Airlines have adapted routes and plans to avoid conflict zones, but the real concern for passengers will be higher fuel prices and longer flights The ripple effects of numerous ongoing conflicts are already being felt and will continue to unfold. stories.title: Crypto-billionaires want 'nothing' for £72m - Reform
stories.summary: Reform UK has insisted its two crypto-billionaire donors want "nothing" in exchange for their combined £72 million gifts to the party. Neither Christopher Harborne nor Ben Delo will be given a knighthood, a peerage or a government contract if Reform comes to power, the party said, after receiving the two gifts in the space of 24 hours. The donations, amounting to £36 million from each man, are the largest in British political history and together are equivalent to three-quarters of the money spent at the 2024 general election by all parties combined. Thailand-based Mr Harborne, Reform’s largest donor, said his gift was "a philanthropic gift to our country" intended to help the party prepare for government. As well as donating to the party, Mr Harborne has given £5 million to Nigel Farage personally, with the Reform leader’s failure to declare the gift leading to an investigation by the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner. Mr Delo, who was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump after a conviction for violating the US Bank Secrecy Act, said his donation was intended to create a "level playing field" for Reform with the other parties.

stories.title: Tielemans frustrated by United's derby defeat display
stories.summary: Youri Tielemans expressed frustration with Manchester United's meek performance in the controversial derby defeat to 10-man Manchester City. Michael Carrick’s men have made a sluggish start to the Premier League season, with a humiliating defeat at Hull, victory against Ipswich and late draw at Everton followed by derby disappointment on Sunday. Phil Foden was sent off for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes midway through the first half but United failed to take advantage, with Erling Haaland’s contentious effort eventually sealing a 1-0 win for City. Pro Ref, the refereeing body, would contact the Red Devils that evening to acknowledge an "error in judgement" in overturning the offside call rather than sending referee Michael Oliver for an on-field review given Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play. United’s fury at the officiating for that decision is as clear as it is understandable, but summer signing Tielemans admits they were not good enough regardless of that moment. "It’s disappointing, so everyone is disappointed and frustrated because we know we can play so much better," the Belgium international told MUTV.

stories.title: No credit in the bank for McGuinness after Kerry slaying
stories.summary: Would he or would he not? In the end, we found out this week that he would. Jim McGuinness has taken up the option of a fourth year in charge of Donegal, in this his second term as manager of the county's senior footballers. Perhaps it is no surprise, given that he will want to atone for how 2026 ended. In many ways Donegal's exit from the championship was somewhat bizarre on the year's longest day. The sun may have been at its highest overlooking Croke Park, but Donegal were deriving little energy from its rays despite taking Dublin to extra-time. It was clear to see that McGuinness's men were finding it a bit of a churn, though credit to them for forcing the additional periods after Michael Murphy nailed a late two-pointer. But it was just delaying the inevitable as the Dubs won with a bit to spare. The camera honed in on Murphy and the question of whether he'll grace the Jones's Road sod again was percolating. Still no word on the 37-year-old's Tír Chonaill future. After what Donegal had done for much of the previous six months, it may not be too hyperbolic to say that their championship exit bordered on the unbelievable - and we are not trying to go all Charlie Haughey GUBU here!

stories.title: South Africa power past New Zealand to seal series win
stories.summary: South Africa scored four second-half tries as they powered to a 43-28 win over New Zealand in Baltimore to wrap up a 3-1 success in their Rugby's Greatest Rivalry Series. The world champions edged to a 17-14 lead at half-time before quickfire close-range tries from Malcolm Marx and Pieter-Steph du Toit swung the match their way. A Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty opened the scoring before All Blacks captain Codie Taylor crossed for an early try, Damian de Allende and Morne van den Berg responding before Will Jordan rounded off 32 phases with a try to cut the interval deficit. Ethan Blackadder pulled a try back after South Africa’s early second-half double, but as they pressed for another score, Kurt-Lee Arendse scooped up a loose ball deep in his own half and carved through a fragmented defence for an individual score. Cameron Hanekom seized on an All Blacks error near their own line to add a sixth try, Beauden Barrett crossing in the dying moments for a late consolation.

stories.summary: Writer, director and composer Bobby Aherne introduces the new seaon below... If, like me, you've spent your life an avid imbiber of all forms of media, then the 'Geography’ section of your brain probably contains an entire atlas of places — largely islands — that don’t actually exist. From Gilligan’s Island to Yoshi’s one, isles Kirrin, Craggy, Monkey, Amity, Trash and Jurassic, and the rocks that hosted Truman Burbank, Mamma Mia! and McGoohan (debatably), we could probably navigate some nonexistent isles better than plenty of real places we’ve actually been to. Listen to the first episode of the latest series of Nero's Class Since yarn-spinners first started making stuff up, islands have proven to be the ideal setting for tall tales and fantastical fiction. See, islands can be whatever you want them to be: a blank canvas for the imagination, a self-contained microcosm of somewhere else, the perfect excuse to take your hero off-grid, and — in the case of somewhere like Summerisle — the most beautiful, picturesque, suffocating prison imaginable. In fiction, islands are almost always seen as a destination for some peace and quiet — two things that they rarely ever provide. I first became savvy to the poetic license provided by islands at some point in the mid-90s. After a family holiday to Inis Oírr, I took to writing a series of stories set somewhere called "Jeegara" — a far-away world made up entirely of 0-150 population islands with names like Jeesh Isle (named after my second class teacher’s favourite PG curse word), Gickile (home to Manure City and Fertiliser Bay), and The Grunki Scatter (your guess is as good as mine). Unfortunately, this creative streak happened to coincide with the opening of the Blanchardstown Centre just around the corner from my house — a development that sparked in me a simultaneous interest in liminal spaces, foreign franchises and mall mapping. In a confusing twist, this meant that all of my meticulously sketched, far-fetched fantasy lands ended up having their very own branches of Tuthills, Roches Stores, Smyths Toys and La Croissanterie. Capitalism had seeped into both the suburbs and my 9-year-old brain, which was seemingly only too eager to also help hoosh it out to a bunch of archipelagos in imaginary distant galaxies.

stories.title: Oasis fans eagerly anticipate tour announcement
stories.summary: Oasis fans are eagerly anticipating a tour announcement later following their drone light show in Manchester on Thursday. The display over the Joie Stadium, home to Manchester City Women, at the Etihad Campus saw the band's logo illuminate before being replaced with the date 14/09/26, and the time 4pm BST. The announcement sparked excitement on social media from fans all hoping they would be able to get tickets. The band also shared a video on their Instagram account on Sunday, further teasing the announcement on Monday. Oasis have been dropping hints about tour venues on social media recently, including Slane Castle, the Etihad Stadium, Celtic Park and Knebworth - where they played to 250,000 people in 1996 during their Britpop heyday. The band reunited for the first time since splitting in 2009 for their successful Live ’25 tour last year.

stories.summary: Queen drummer Roger Taylor walked the Vin + Omi runway alongside Bake Off's Alison Hammond and Prue Leith ahead of London Fashion Week. The 77-year-old musician was the first celebrity to emerge at the eco-conscious designers’ Anarchy show, wearing black trousers, bright red high-top trainers and a black velvet jacket streaked with rust-coloured bleach marks. His trademark dark sunglasses remained firmly in place – perhaps unsurprisingly, given that Vin said ahead of the show that Taylor’s transformation was never going to be particularly dramatic. "Roger’s going to look like himself with a different jacket," Vin told the Press Association with a laugh. "We couldn’t stick a wig on Roger and make him look like part of the show because he would freak out. I think, and quite rightly so, I mean, it’s always more difficult with blokes because they’re more rigid." After completing his turn on the runway, Taylor took his place on the front row alongside his wife, where he remained for the rest of the lengthy show.

stories.title: Trump tariff move a late winning goal for Govt at Doonbeg
stories.summary: Irish politics and sport often blend but nothing might replicate Donald Trump's whirlwind 28 hours of golf, diplomacy and trade at the Irish Open in Doonbeg. The US President’s visit to Ireland ended with a major win for the Government, as he used his speech at Shane Lowry’s prizegiving ceremony to announce he would remove tariffs from Irish whiskey. It’s understood that the Taoiseach had raised the issue during his meeting with Mr Trump at Farmleigh House and on a number of occasions over the weekend including at lunch in Doonbeg on Sunday, with Irish whiskey subject to a 10% tariff contrasted to a zero tariff on whiskey coming from Northern Ireland. Government ministers and diplomats could not have dreamed for a better outcome at a time when Ireland’s influence in America has been diminishing and with several of Trump’s administration far from favourable towards the Irish. The announcement – and its ties to Shane Lowry who joked distillers should start sending him cheques – demonstrates how Ireland can use soft diplomacy to punch above its weight at an international level. However, it will be interesting to note the response in Brussels at a time when Ireland is hosting the EU Presidency. The shock tariff announcement will be a boost for Micheál Martin, who has derived a tangible gain from his time in Mr Trump’s company over the weekend.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has turned his focus to golf after triggering a diplomatic row as he backed a united Ireland on the first day of his trip to the country. Speaking to reporters this afternoon, the US president claimed Irish reunification was inevitable, adding it "may as well happen now". Mr Trump's visit to Ireland also led to protests in a number of locations, with thousands flooding the streets of Dublin city centre to express their anger. After a series of engagements in Dublin in the morning, Mr Trump travelled to the Doonbeg golf resort he owns in Co Clare where he watched some of the action at the Irish Open with his family. He was given a rapturous reception as he made a brief appearance in the members’ bar of the hotel. Punters cheered and chanted "USA" and sang songs as Mr Trump filed through the bar tonight.

stories.summary: President Catherine Connolly has said that she conveyed to the US president the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted. The meeting in Phoenix Park did not have video cameras in the room but there were members of delegations present. Following a ceremonial welcome, including the signing of the Distinguished Visitors Book, the playing of the National Anthems, and the Inspection of a Guard of Honour, the two presidents met in the President’s Drawing Room. In a statement following the meeting, President Connolly said: "As President of Ireland, I am very conscious that Ireland and the United States of America are bound by strong ties. "This is a deep connection, built over centuries, which allows us to speak openly to one another.

stories.title: Trump says US should have world's lowest interest rates
stories.summary: No country should have lower interest rates than the US, President Donald Trump said yesterday, days before the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting. Speaking to reporters at the Irish Open golf tournament, Trump said he did not know whether Fed policymakers will raise interest rates at their meeting this week. But he said the US "should be paying the lowest interest rate in the world" no matter what the Federal Reserve's data indicates about inflation and the economy. The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index, a key measure of underlying inflation, on Friday posted its largest increase in four months. That reinforced expectations that the US Fed will raise the target range for its federal funds rate, now at 3.5% to 3.75%, at the conclusion of its Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Wednesday. stories.title: Six dead, 130 missing after Indonesian ferry capsizes
stories.summary: Rescuers in Indonesia said at least six people were killed and 130 others were missing after a ferry sailing between the islands of Java and Borneo was hit by bad weather and capsized. The Virgo Transport 8, carrying 243 passengers and crew, had lost contact with its shipping company early today after departing from Surabaya in east Java. Basarnas, Indonesia's national search and rescue agency, said in its latest update that six people were killed and 130 were missing. It said 107 people had been rescued. There were 213 passengers and 30 crew members on board, the agency added. Indonesian Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said the ship had capsized. "From the information we received, based on helicopter surveillance... the ship capsized but has not sunk. As of 3pm (local time) it had not sunk yet, but it was capsized," he said at a news conference in Banjarmasin.

stories.title: Shelton wants service rule change after US Open defeat
stories.summary: Beaten US Open finalist Ben Shelton has called for a change to a "stupid" rule after being told he had to stand in position while Alexander Zverev bounces the ball. Zverev's service routine has irked a number of players this fortnight, with the German bouncing the ball up to 25 times before starting his serving motion. While there is a 25-second rule for a first serve, there is none for a second serve. Shelton was annoyed at being told by umpire Marijana Veljovic that he should be standing on the line ready to recieve, even though the serve might not come for another 30 seconds. "I think there’s not an athlete in the world that you’re going to watch them do their thing and they’re going to sit in a ready position for 30 seconds before the play starts," said the 23-year-old American. "So for me it’s the same. I’m not going to sit there in a ready position with my knees bent, tension in my body for 30 seconds while I’m waiting.
